items.title: 2026 is an exciting year for the Rust compiler (and me)
items.summary: Article URL: https://yoyo-code.com/2026-is-exciting-year-for-rust-compiler-and-me/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50166502 Points: 117 # Comments: 41
items.content:
You might have already noticed that 2026 seems to be a bit special year for Rust compiler. It seems like there's just a lot of stuff going on. Some things were already announced since I started writing this, but there's still a bunch more that's not as visible. I'll share some things that I personally find interesting.

To explain a bit of context, what happened this year is that multiple different initiatives are reaching final steps at the same time. In other words, 2026 is not that special with the amount of work being done, but it's a year when we see several long-term investments starting to pay dividends.

Probably the biggest thing is the next generation trait solver . This is a reimplementation of a big part of the type system, and it has been in the works for a very long time - Almost 10 years in various forms. It fixes a bunch of soundness bugs and unblocks a lot of features and fixes for long-standing issues.

It's easy to understate how big of a deal this is for the compiler. This work resolves a major piece of technical debt that a lot of compiler developers dreamed about for years. It also frees up a bunch of people with a fresh and deep understanding of the type system to work on new things. The queue of things that get unblocked includes many common pain points of the language, even things that might seem benign or unrelated. It contains solutions to big problems in async Rust, or various limitations of impl Trait .

Another big thing is Polonius, a new borrow checker implementation , long time in the making as well. It enables more code to compile and unblocks several related features - including (hopefully one day) internal references. The compiler impact of this is not as big as with the new solver, but it's still a pretty big deal.

My main area of interest is compiler performance, and here we have quite a few things going on. After 1-2 years of a sort of stagnation (at least in terms of results), we suddenly have a lot of things going on at once. So much so that I have a hard time remembering everything, but from the top of my head:

Very old initiative that was put a few years on hiatus with many unclear blockers. The development restarted again a few years ago with a new contributor @SparrowLi , and over time a number of other people contributed to the effort.

Over the years, this turned out to be a massive can of worms. I get the feeling that almost nobody is really happy with the design. However, there doesn't seem to be a better alternative for the foreseeable future, and parallel frontend is highly desirable, so the solution ended up being just grinding through a number of annoying and hairy problems until there's nothing left.

The current project goal is driven by @petrochenkov and is getting close to stabilization.

LLVM 23 was unambiguous and unexpectedly large positive change in performance. For a long time, LLVM upgrades were not particularly great for rustc performance. This changed after LLVM 10 upgrade, which introduced a massive 10% regression, and @nikic , current lead developer of LLVM, called it out in his blog post, Make LLVM fast again . In the post he also introduced a system for tracking LLVM performance over time, inspired by the one we use for rustc .

Since then, LLVM started catching performance regressions earlier, and results for upgrades in rustc went from "less bad", to "somewhat mixed", to "mostly positive with caveats." The last one of those was LLVM 22, which was green on icount benchmarks, but almost universally red on wall time.

LLVM 23 is pretty much entirely positive. I don't follow LLVM development that much, but my understanding is that this is because there's now more work on actually optimizing it, as opposed to working on features without trying to regress performance. These days the improvements come both from new optimizations (those help optimize the compiler during bootstrap) and from LLVM itself getting faster.

Compiler performance has been on a steady streak of improvements in the past few months. There's probably no single explanation for it, just a combination of new contributors coming in, old contributors getting to do more perf work, and tooling improvements combined with architectural cleanups unlocking new opportunities.

With more people working in this area, I've noticed a lot of cross-pollination, where a certain idea would circle around a few people's minds, as people get inspired by each other's PRs and try related things.

I also feel like we got a lot better at managing regressions - triaging and addressing them. This is partially a tooling investment, but also a lot about processes and social structures. A major development here is the connection between tree ops and perf triage, represented notably by @JonathanBrouwer .

This means that people who manage merges often directly triage their performance impact. This is important because it shrinks the response time, but the connection is useful for other reasons as well. The perf impact informs how you group PRs into rollups , for example. Turns out that Conway's law is still a law.

I also greatly enjoy helping people interpreting the measurement results and diagnose regressions. I often find that even just a few sentences from somebody who's been looking at the results every day for many years go a long way towards getting the regression addressed.

All in all, I feel like the compile time concerns are integrated into the development better than they have ever been.

This seemingly came out of nowhere earlier this year, and it's quite interesting. @Amanieu proposed a MIR optimization pass that allows the compiler to eliminate copies that LLVM has trouble optimizing. It speeds up both compile time and runtime.

This is one of those passes that makes sense to implement in MIR instead of LLVM, because the Rust part of the compiler has better information about whether it's valid to apply specifically for Rust. Even more so because it actually requires changing the MIR semantics a bit.

It matters for Rust in particular because Rust typically generates more moves than C(++), which is the primary LLVM target.

This one is particularly close to my heart because I've been following the efforts for a very long time. Polymorphization is one of the most impactful compiler performance optimizations we could ever do, but it's unfortunately really tricky to implement.

This would be the third experiment I'm aware of. This time it's slightly different from the previous ones, and it's inspired by a similar mechanism in Swift.

The difference is that the original polymorphization intends to only avoid duplicate or redundant monomorphizations, so it's purely a compile time optimization with no runtime impact, while the Swift-style one intends to polymorphize everything and pass around layouts of generic parameters as arguments. This will have a runtime cost, so it'll be something you can tweak with compiler flags.

If my understanding is still up to date, next-solver will also enable polymorphization in the previously intended way. Either way, both options run into the same problems, so the work is useful for both. It's also possible that both options come out of this same effort. Either way, this is still just an experiment with a bunch of problems to solve, so we'll have to wait to see how it turns out. The project goal has been proposed and driven by @camelid .

@blyxyas is working on a project goal , which will enable cargo to share artifacts between cargo check and cargo build . The goal is actually more general, but this is probably its most recognizable outcome. This is something we wanted for ages, so it's really cool to see progress on this front.

This was already announced , and it will shrink the target directory size by 5-30%, depending on the workload.

Already announced as well , this is another project that has been in the works for quite some time. As with the other things above, this is major internal restructuring that unlocks other things - namely granular locking of the target directory and cross-workspace caching.

@bjorn3 has been working on fixing support for these two flags, which enable pipelining of build scripts and proc macros. As you can see in the proposal , this is yet another line of work that boils down to fixing a laundry list of internal issues and architectural problems until suddenly a big thing is unlocked.

There have been a number of initiatives in the compiler architecture. I'll mention a few, just to (once again) underscore the point that big things don't happen in big-bang projects coming out of nowhere, but rather as consequences of sustained long-term investments into a healthy system.

Two years ago, @jdonszelmann started the effort to unify and cleanup how attributes are represented and checked in the compiler. Just a few days ago, the last remaining attribute was ported to the new system. This significantly improves how attributes are checked and unblocks improvements to diagnostics and other things.

Earlier this year, @Zalathar and @nnethercote cleaned up the implementation of rustc's query system. This improved performance but more importantly, made the system easier to understand, which was often a blocker for making improvements to it. The system is still a pretty scary part of the codebase, but this is a big step forward.

items.title: Auto termiche in UE anche dopo il 2035: più vicino ulteriore compromesso
items.summary: PPE, S&D e Renew avrebbero raggiunto un’intesa per allentare i futuri limiti sulle emissioni. Il compromesso potrebbe consentire nuove immatricolazioni con motore a combustione anche dopo il 2035, ma l’accordo non è ancora definitivo ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Il cosiddetto stop europeo alle nuove auto con motore a combustione dal 2035 potrebbe essere ulteriormente ridimensionato. Nel Parlamento Europeo i negoziatori dei tre principali gruppi centristi – Partito Popolare Europeo, Socialisti e Democratici e Renew Europe – hanno raggiunto nella notte un compromesso sulla revisione dei limiti di emissioni per le nuove automobili.

Secondo un documento visionato dallo Spiegel , la proposta prevede per il 2035 una riduzione delle emissioni allo scarico del 95% rispetto ai livelli del 2021, con la possibilità di scendere a un obiettivo effettivo dell’87,5% attraverso crediti legati all’utilizzo di acciaio prodotto con minori emissioni. Altre ricostruzioni sintetizzano quindi il compromesso proprio come una riduzione dell’87,5%. In entrambi i casi, rispetto all’attuale obiettivo del 100%, resterebbe margine per vendere anche dopo il 2035 alcune nuove auto ibride e con motore a combustione.

Per ora l’intesa riguarda per ora i negoziatori dei tre gruppi politici e dovrà superare diversi passaggi parlamentari prima di poter diventare la posizione ufficiale dell’Europarlamento.

Il primo banco di prova sarà giovedì prossimo, il 22 ottobre, quando le commissioni Trasporti e Industria del Parlamento Europeo dovrebbero esprimersi sul pacchetto. La commissione Ambiente, competente sul dossier, dovrebbe seguirle all’inizio di novembre, mentre il voto dell’intera assemblea è atteso a dicembre. Solo dopo dovrà essere trovata un’intesa anche con gli Stati membri. La normativa segue infatti la procedura legislativa europea ordinaria e la posizione del Parlamento dovrà confrontarsi con quella del Consiglio.

La regola attualmente in vigore continua a prevedere dal 2035 una riduzione del 100% delle emissioni di anidride carbonica allo scarico per le nuove auto e i nuovi furgoni, equivalente a un obiettivo di 0 g/km.

Con l’Automotive Package presentato a dicembre, Bruxelles aveva già proposto di sostituire l’obiettivo del 100% con una riduzione del 90% delle emissioni allo scarico dal 2035. Il restante 10% avrebbe dovuto essere compensato attraverso l’impiego di acciaio europeo a basse emissioni oppure di carburanti come e-fuel e biocarburanti.

La Commissione aveva esplicitamente indicato che questo meccanismo avrebbe consentito di mantenere un ruolo dopo il 2035 non soltanto per ibride plug-in e veicoli dotati di range extender, quindi un motore termico che mantiene la carica della batteria; ma anche per mild hybrid e vetture puramente termiche. Insomma, l'attuale proposta è un ulteriore compromesso della visione originale.

Parallelamente si sta muovendo anche il fronte degli Stati membri. Germania e Francia hanno raggiunto di recente una posizione comune che prevede una riduzione del 90% delle emissioni entro il 2035, senza l’obbligo di compensare integralmente il restante 10% attraverso acciaio verde o combustibili alternativi.

L’accordo tra Berlino e Parigi potrebbe avere un peso rilevante nella costruzione della posizione del Consiglio, anche se sarà comunque necessario raccogliere una maggioranza qualificata tra gli Stati membri.

Francia e Germania stanno negoziando anche su requisiti "Made in Europe", sostegno all’industria locale e accesso agli incentivi, con Parigi particolarmente interessata a rafforzare i criteri legati alla produzione europea.

Comunqu la revisione delle regole sul 2035 è soltanto una parte dell’Automotive Package. La Commissione vuole utilizzare i cosiddetti "super crediti" per favorire le piccole elettriche economiche prodotte in Europa. La nuova categoria riguarda auto lunghe non più di 4,2 metri: vendere questi modelli dovrebbe pesare maggiormente nel calcolo delle emissioni medie della gamma di un costruttore, incentivando così l’arrivo di un maggior numero di veicoli elettrici compatti.

Sono previste anche maggiore flessibilità per gli obiettivi intermedi del 2030 e misure specifiche per i furgoni, settore nel quale la Commissione ha già proposto di ridurre dal 50 al 40% il target di abbattimento delle emissioni previsto per quell’anno. Dal 2030 Bruxelles punta ad accelerare l’elettrificazione delle flotte aziendali attraverso obiettivi nazionali per veicoli a zero e basse emissioni, lasciando poi ai singoli Stati la scelta degli strumenti da utilizzare.

items.title: La Romania ha di nuovo un governo dopo sei mesi di crisi politica
items.summary: Luca Niculescu, il quarto primo ministro nominato dal presidente Nicușor Dan, ha faticosamente ottenuto la fiducia del parlamento
items.content:
Martedì il parlamento romeno ha dato la fiducia a Luca Niculescu per insediare un governo di minoranza, chiudendo così sei mesi di crisi politica. Niculescu è il quarto primo ministro nominato dal presidente europeista Nicușor Dan dall’inizio della crisi. Gli altri tre indicati non erano riusciti a trovare il sostegno sufficiente. Niculescu, che è un diplomatico e ha un profilo tecnico, ha ottenuto 280 voti a favore dal parlamento in seduta comune e 58 contro.

La crisi di governo era iniziata ad aprile , quando i Socialdemocratici (di sinistra ma con posizioni conservatrici su temi sociali) erano usciti dal governo e poi a maggio avevano votato con l’estrema destra dell’Alleanza per l’unità dei romeni (AUR) una mozione di sfiducia all’allora primo ministro Ilie Bolojan, facendo cadere il governo. Sono il partito con più seggi in parlamento e sono stati decisivi perché Niculescu potesse insediarsi. Il governo è sostenuto anche dal Partito Nazional Liberale (PNL) di centrodestra, di cui è leader Bolojan, e dal partito della minoranza ungherese (UDMR).

I Socialdemocratici contestavano a Bolojan l’eccessivo rigore economico e sostenevano di essere disposti a tornare nella vecchia coalizione a patto di cambiare primo ministro. Finora però non si erano messi d’accordo con gli altri partiti. Hanno sostenuto Niculescu ufficialmente per evitare che la crisi si protraesse, ma sono l’unico partito che partecipa direttamente al nuovo governo, con 11 ministri , che per il resto è tecnico. Il PNL ha detto di aver scelto di appoggiarlo per evitare elezioni anticipate che probabilmente sarebbero state vinte da AUR.

Niculescu è un ex giornalista radiofonico e tra il 2016 e il 2022 era stato ambasciatore in Francia, in seguito era stato inviato speciale della Romania per l’OCSE (l’Organizzazione per la cooperazione e lo sviluppo economico, che si occupa di studi e analisi su economia e società). Martedì, durante il dibattito in parlamento, ha rivendicato la sua estrazione: «Oggi sono state usate molte etichette. Non sono un politico, non mi unirò a questa sarabanda di dichiarazioni affilate. Non vi sto chiedendo un assegno in bianco, vi sto chiedendo di capire che alla Romania serve un governo».

Niculescu ha detto che martedì terrà la prima riunione del governo. Il suo obiettivo dichiarato è approvare una legge di bilancio per il 2026 e impostare quella del 2027, con l’obiettivo di ridurre il deficit. I Socialdemocratici hanno posto la condizione che la legge di bilancio di quest’anno sia approvata entro inizio dicembre, e potrebbero esserci nuove tensioni coi partiti che sostengono il governo.

I Socialdemocratici erano stati citati nel caso di Kimberly Guilfoyle , l’ambasciatrice statunitense in Grecia che si è dimessa la settimana scorsa. Guilfoyle aveva sostenuto, probabilmente con una certa esagerazione, che lei e gli Stati Uniti avessero avuto un ruolo nella caduta del governo di Bolojan dopo incontri con dirigenti dei Socialdemocratici. La necessità di avere un governo pienamente funzionante è stata acuita dal moltiplicarsi degli attacchi russi alle navi mercantili nel mar Nero, al largo di Romania e Bulgaria.

items.title: How I got over 300 Tor exit nodes removed
items.summary: Article URL: https://kaba.cx/posts/20261020_Tor/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50166257 Points: 245 # Comments: 60
items.content:
On Friday Oct 2, 09:35am, 333 infected exit nodes started a coordinated campaign to intercept SSH connections and gather as much unencrypted data as possible.

To give you a sense of scale, all of Tor has around 3000 exit relays, so roughly 10% were under their control.

The attackers had gained access to the servers two months earlier, in August, and quietly deployed their Ebury 1.8.3 payload (an OpenSSH backdoor and credential stealer for Linux).

By blocking certain ports, they made their exit nodes handle only unencrypted mail traffic. An interesting writeup by one of the victims (a veteran Tor operator) goes into great detail about that: lists.torproject.org/mailman3

In this post I'll focus on the second attack, the SSH MITM. If you happen to get a circuit that exits over one of those 333 infected exit nodes, you won't notice anything at first. Encrypted web traffic is forwarded as usual, but if you attempt an SSH connection over Port 22, you're unknowingly redirected to one of 12 SSH interception servers.

That's exactly what happened to me on Friday morning. My SSH connection got redirected, and I was greeted with this warning:

But if you ignore the warning and go ahead with the login, the attacker does three things:

On Friday evening I contacted the Tor Project's network health team with my findings. They confirmed this was something new and got to work by contacting the affected relay operators.

In their announcement, the health team described the pattern:

You can see the impact of those 333 exit nodes being shut down. On metrics.torproject.org a clear dip is visible on October 4th and has not recovered since.

Consider running a relay: community.torproject.org/relay/setup/

In this part I'll go into detail about how I found all the infected exit nodes.

Using exitmap , I built a simple script that did the following: it pinned an exit node, then opened an SSH connection from my server A to my server B.

I ran the script against every single one of the ~3000 exit relays. Around a dozen served a fake fingerprint, and over 300 didn't intercept anything but redirected through those same interception servers. Redirecting alone was enough to confirm the exit was infected.

In some further analysis I used sshesame as a honeypot. Tricking the MITM into logging into the honeypot showed that they used paramiko (a Python SSH library) and also how they attempted to install Ebury using Perl.

Checking for permissions first, then executing a base64-encoded command.

The biggest question is still how they got into all those servers in the first place. One theory is that the hosting company itself was hacked (discussed here: lists.torproject.org ). But that's just a theory floating around. In truth, no one really knows.

Another is who's behind it. The use of Ebury and the broad collection of unencrypted data point to a financially motivated crime group. Though this too is just speculation.

I also suspect they deliberately launched their attack on a Friday, hoping that no one would want to ruin their weekend by responding. All the more credit to the Tor Team for acting so quickly!

The lesson is the same as always: extra security is a worthwhile investment. Disable password authentication in favor of ssh keys. I for one am going to buy myself some hardware keys today. :)

items.title: Huge setback for Alberta's separatist movement after decisive defeat
items.summary: Leaders of the movement for independence vow to push on but the margin of defeat could make that difficult.
items.content:
It was a decisive result in a referendum that could have strained the bonds of national unity.

But preliminary results show that more than two-thirds of Alberta voters sent a clear message that they want to remain in Canada.

It's possible that once the final tally is counted, the rejection by a comfortable majority of voters to pursue separation through a binding referendum could halt Alberta's separatist sentiment in its tracks.

This would push the idea that had been discussed quietly for decades back into the political fringes.

For leaders of the Alberta separatist movement, while the result was expected given the polling, it was still disappointing after more than a year of campaigning and pushing for a vote on separation.

Asked by the BBC how he felt in one sentence after the results, separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre simply said: "Not happy".

The outcome was celebrated almost immediately by Prime Minister Mark Carney, who said in a statement that "Albertans made a clear choice".

But the movement's leaders say their battle is long from over and that the issue could dominate Alberta politics for years to come.

Jeffrey Rath, a Calgary-lawyer and one of the main spokespeople for Alberta separation, said he and others "plan to roll up our sleeves and work harder".

Keith Wilson, another separatist, told supporters in Calgary that while the vote is over, "the conversation about Alberta's future in Canada and our place in Canada and our role in Canada will continue".

Smith, who openly supported and campaigned for the unity vote, thanked voters for the result.

The Alberta premier has been criticised for taking a "dangerous" gamble that the independence push would likely face defeat while still giving her restive base what they wanted.

She lowered the petition threshold needed to get the citizen-led campaign the ballot in the first place.

How oil-rich Alberta's economy might fare if it broke away from Canada

Carney pitches oil pipeline as a response to US-Canada trade war

At Canada's biggest rodeo, the starting gun is fired in the fight over Alberta separation

By making Monday's result non-binding, she got around a court decision blocking the pro-separation petition because it failed to consult indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected if the province separated.

That gamble could test her leadership of the United Conservative Party, which she has led since 2022.

Albertans who voted against an independence referendum told the BBC throughout the campaign that they were motivated by a desire to keep the country united, especially as Canada grapples with tariff threats from the US, its longtime ally.

They also feared that an independent Alberta could be vulnerable to outside influence - or even annexation.

Thomas Lukaszuk, a prominent pro-unity campaigner, told a crowd of supporters on Monday night that the early results made him proud to be Albertan.

At a pro-unity results watch party in Edmonton, Lukaszuk appealled directly to separatists, saying that "some of the issues they have raised are legitimate", and that the province must do the hard work of healing the divisions laid bare by this debate.

"I don't want to see us doing another referendum like this ever again," Lukaszuk said.

Premier Smith told CBC earlier in the week that she would not hold an independence referendum if Albertans vote against it as long as she is premier.

The separatist sentiment has its roots in "western alienation" which is a term that has been used for decades by some in Canada's western provinces to describe a feeling of being ignored or overlooked by the federal government in central Canada.

Alberta independence supporters - and many on the unity side - believe that Ottawa has long undermined the province's oil and gas industry, most recently through environmental policies.

That anger later deepened as some Albertans grew frustrated with the response by former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau to the Covid-19 pandemic and vaccine mandates, viewing them as yet another example of government overreach.

Carney, who was raised in Alberta, has worked with Smith to address some of these issues, signing an agreement that would see a new pipeline from Alberta built to Canada's pacific coast.

He nodded to that in his statement on Monday night, saying that his plan is to unlock Canada's "full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta at its core".

But there are signs that there could be tension in the future between Carney and Smith, an able politician and a survivor - so far - of Alberta's rough and tumble politics.

She also put nine other questions to Albertans on Monday, most that seek to give the province more autonomy from Ottawa, including on matters like immigration.

The (very) preliminary results suggest that many might pass.

Some who voted in favour of a second binding separation referendum have said they didn't want outright independence, but some leverage over Ottawa. Smith has said these other nine questions help give her just that.

Quebec, another province with similar sovereigntist sentiments, could offer clues on where Alberta's separation movement might end up.

They held two separation referendums, in 1980 and 1995, both of which were defeated by a close margin.

Alberta independence supporters don't hide the fact that they gain inspiration from the majority French-speaking province.

They view Quebec as having successfully used the threat of separation to gain significantly more autonomy over provincial affairs.

And despite support for Quebec sovereignty being at historic lows, a newly elected provincial government has pledged to hold a third referendum on independence by 2030.

The sovereigntist Parti Quebecois "has just formed the government of Quebec with 28% of the vote," he said.

"It's not out of the realm of possibility", he added, that Alberta separatists could do the same in the future.

items.title: Kenya cult leader's children still being starved weeks before trial, son says
items.summary: Dan Mackenzie initially defended his father but now says he felt he had to report his own grandmother.
items.content:
The eldest son of Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie, convicted of murdering 191 people, says his younger siblings were still being forced to fast as recently as two weeks ago.

Dan Mackenzie, 27, said he reported the case to police, who rescued eight children, including his five younger siblings from their grandmother's house, and took them to a rescue centre.

"They were basically forcibly fasted because they were denying food to them for almost three days," he tells BBC's Newsday.

His father was found guilty on Monday of murdering 190 children and one adult who starved to death in Shakahola forest, near the Kenyan coast.

He had ordered members of his doomsday cult to starve themselves and their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

Twenty-eight other cult leaders were also convicted of murder.

Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders

Dan Mackenzie, who had initially defended his father, said at first he had struggled to understand the allegations against the cult leader, but came to realise the scale of the tragedy during the court proceedings.

"When I was 12, I was forced to fast for almost a week," he says. He also remembers church members beating him for hours to make him attend a service as a child.

Now, he says he felt he had to report family members who still believe in the teachings in order to free his siblings. "I had to report my grandmother."

The cult leader's doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil".

Now living in the coastal town of Malindi, Dan earns a living as a motorcycle taxi driver, supporting himself and his younger siblings.

He said some people in the town had been angry with him because of his father's crimes, but others "had accepted him because he had distanced himself from that life".

"I hope the verdict would bring some comfort to those who had lost friends and relatives," Dan tells BBC's Newsday.

On Monday, Stephen Mwiti, 48, who said he had lost all six of his children to the cult, welcomed the verdict.

"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court.

His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.

Delivering her eight-hour judgment in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".

One of his co-accused told the court that Mackenzie had said anyone who resisted fasting must be forced to go to heaven "through kicks and blows".

Burials in the forest where the cult was based were described as "weddings", with those who died celebrated as having "wedded with Jesus", the judge said.

Mackenzie and other cult leaders also face separate cases involving terrorism, radicalisation and denying children an education.

The murder verdict is the first ruling on the most serious charges against the pastor, who was arrested in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were discovered in shallow graves in Shakahola forest, near Kenya's coast.

'I fear for my sons': Mother awaits DNA results on remains linked to Kenya's starvation cult

items.title: Tsrs: A Port of TypeScript to Rust
items.summary: Article URL: https://blog.cloudflare.com/typescript-rust-port/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50165953 Points: 261 # Comments: 122
items.content:
Cloudflare and VoidZero are now working with Max Schwenk of Owner.com on tsrs , a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler. We are doing this work in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, and incubating tsrs as part of the Oxc JavaScript compiler toolchain .

Our goal is to help developers spend less time waiting for their code to be checked and more time building. Making TypeScript faster and more memory-efficient also helps bring complete development environments to more places, including right in your browser.

To be clear, we are not forking TypeScript. We believe the TypeScript team should remain in full control of the language’s design and direction. They have maintained a long-term vision while guiding TypeScript’s adoption across the JavaScript community. We do not want to change that.

The TypeScript team can move quite fast on many things, but for some features they may spend years intentionally exploring options and making prototypes before picking the right implementation. A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible. We have to preserve the TypeScript language strictly based on its original implementation – and the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like.

Early benchmarks of our Rust port of TypeScript are promising: tsrs is up to 8x faster and uses ~70% less memory compared to TypeScript 7.0 when using the same number of type check workers:

As you can see, the next version of TypeScript already brings many performance improvements, making TypeScript 7.1 beta up to 2.5x faster than TypeScript 7.0. Some of these optimizations were upstreamed from tsrs , and we’re hoping to find more.

You may have seen recent benchmarks of different TypeScript ports with various performance claims, often due to using larger machine types and different options compared to TypeScript’s defaults. We worked with the TypeScript team to ensure the above benchmarks are comparing the same configuration.

By default, tsrs ships with an adaptive configuration dependent on the machine type that uses more memory but is even faster:

TypeScript in Rust aims to be a faithful port of TypeScript. You can try an experimental release by installing the tsrs package from npm:

We’ve seen many attempts at porting TypeScript to other languages over the years. Because of the complexity involved, only one of the ports succeeded: the TypeScript team’s port of TypeScript from JavaScript to Go.

However, frontier AI models can now do large-scale ports almost independently in a matter of days. We have now seen slopforks, faithful ports, and completely re-architected versions of TypeScript in Rust or C++. There is clearly a demand for even faster TypeScript.

You might be thinking: “TypeScript’s Go port already made TypeScript 10x faster and far more memory efficient than the previous version written in TypeScript. Why isn’t that enough?”

However, it’s not just about speed. Rust offers some unique advantages: running in WebAssembly . The Rust + Wasm story has always been strong, and one of the reasons comes down to the fundamentals of Rust’s language design. When you compile a Go program to Wasm, you have to compile Go’s garbage collector along with it. But Rust’s memory management model enables straightforward memory interactions between a WebAssembly guest and host. This is one of the key things that makes Rust a much better fit for the WebAssembly use-case: memory efficiency.

Cloudflare Workers have supported Wasm for a long time. Just a few weeks ago we announced supporting native Rust in Workers with the new Emscripten target for wasm-bindgen. When you run entire software build and deployment systems in tight loops on Workers, the benefits of a small memory footprint pay off quickly. It means you can run these workloads so efficiently that it’s now possible to run fully encapsulated development systems in places where they couldn’t have been run before.

This enables new possibilities when combined with agents: You are now able to run a development toolchain end-to-end in a fully sandboxed environment on Cloudflare. But with Wasm, you can also run those environments safely client-side in your browser, or on an embedded device, or an IoT application.

First, we are working with Theo Browne to merge tsc-rs and tsrs into a single package that supports all of TypeScript’s features including Language Server Protocol (LSP) and content mappers. Second, we’ve seen a lot of success with how we maintain Vinext in sync with its upstream, Next.js. We explained how we do this in a recent blog post :

We will apply the same process to TypeScript, taking extreme care that we don’t introduce diverging behaviors from upstream TypeScript. When we come across performance improvements, we’ll attempt to contribute them back to the TypeScript Go codebase so everyone wins.

Finally, we recognize that there are some differences to the upstream version of TypeScript right now, like for example the order in which diagnostics are printed. We aim to reduce those differences to a minimum by the time we publish a stable release.

Cloudflare is already the home of many free and open source Rust tools that power the JavaScript ecosystem, such as Vite, Rolldown, Oxlint, and Oxfmt. With more than 10 million developers building on Cloudflare, we care a lot about making the underlying developer toolchain faster, more portable, and easier to run in more places. We are excited to experiment with deeper tsrs integrations into our stack, for example for type-aware lint rules in Oxlint.

Like with Vinext, our goal is to run tsrs as a well-maintained healthy open source project — without getting in the way of TypeScript itself. The Oxc team has already begun refactoring the codebase to make it faster, use less memory, and make it maintainable. We know the TypeScript team is taking this seriously – they are experimenting with memory and performance improvements for tsc . We are excited to collaborate with the TypeScript team and the JavaScript community to build the best and fastest implementations of TypeScript together.

items.title: Jepsen: Orkes Conductor 5.3.2
items.summary: Article URL: https://jepsen.io/analyses/orkes-conductor-5.3.2 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50165904 Points: 30 # Comments: 0
items.content:
A workflow orchestrator is a software system which executes computations made up of small tasks . Tasks are connected in a workflow , which routes the outputs of some tasks to the inputs of others, determines which tasks may be scheduled and when, and so on. The orchestrator manages workflows and specific executions of them, runs their tasks, persists state, and tries to drive each execution to completion.

Conductor is a workflow system originally built by Netflix and open sourced in 2016. 1 The open source version, Conductor OSS , is now maintained by the Conductor OSS Foundation . This foundation is led by Orkes , whose founders helped build Conductor at Netflix. Orkes also offers a hosted version of Conductor with additional features, called Orkes Conductor . This analysis focuses on Orkes Conductor, which we call Conductor for short.

In Conductor, a workflow definition is a JSON structure that defines which tasks must be executed, their order, what their inputs and outputs should be, and so on. Each workflow definition is identified by a name and a version. For example, a workflow definition could specify that to adopt a cat, one must first complete an application, then schedule a vet visit, and receive vaccination records from the vet. A workflow may also accept an input (say, the name of the cat) and produce an output (like a certificate of adoption).

A workflow definition may be run many times—say, once for each cat to be adopted. Each instance is called a workflow execution , but we often call an execution a “workflow” for short. Each execution is identified by a unique workflow ID . During an execution a task may also be attempted multiple times (e.g. in case of failure), and each attempt receives a unique execution ID .

Some tasks are built into Conductor. Some are system tasks , like making HTTP requests or submitting events to a log like Kafka. Others are called operators —these provide control flow like conditionals, fork/join, loops, and so on. Operators may execute ECMAScript code to perform user-defined logic. Finally there are worker tasks , which are written by users to perform the “business logic” of the system.

To start an execution of a workflow, one can make an API call to Conductor, submit an event through a message broker, or use Conductor’s built-in cron -style scheduler. Once acknowledged, Conductor schedules the workflow’s tasks and attempts to drive it to completion.

Conductor has five major components . Conductor servers are stateless processes which manage workflows and schedule execution. They provide an API and user interface, interact with external services, and track state. The definitions of workflows, the state of their executions and the results of tasks are stored in a database like Postgres, Cassandra, or Redis. Conductor also uses a queue—often Redis—to dispatch work to various processes, and to store short-lived state. Finally, there are two pools of stateless workers: standard workers which execute Conductor’s built-in tasks, and custom workers, which are written by users using SDKs for various languages . All workers connect to a Conductor server , poll the server for tasks, execute them, and send results back to the server.

Each component may be scaled independently. Any number of servers and workers can run concurrently, and nodes may be killed and restarted at any time. In version 5.3.2, the database and queue were both required to preserve all acknowledged writes. However, version 5.4.0 introduced a new option which enabled the use of a lossy storage system for all queues except for the main decider queue .

Conductor guarantees “at least once message delivery” , ensuring that all messages are persistent and will be delivered to task workers one or more times. Conductor also guarantees that workflows eventually terminate. “If a workflow has started, it will run to completion as long as all its tasks are completed.” This does not necessarily mean that workflows and tasks execute successfully. Tasks can run out of retry attempts , fail with non-retryable errors, or be explicitly canceled—and a similar state machine applies to workflow executions. However, workflows should eventually converge on a terminal status : COMPLETED , FAILED , TIMED_OUT , or TERMINATED .

When tasks are executed, each attempt receives a unique execution ID, and also a unique retry count , which indicates the number of attempts already performed .

Orkes says that for each workflow execution, each instance of a task has at most one visible successful execution. Tasks may execute successfully multiple times—for instance, if a Conductor server loses its connection to the database just before persisting the completion of the task execution. However, once the output of a successful task becomes visible, no task, workflow, or API call will observe a different output. 2

To verify these properties, we built a test harness for Orkes Conductor using the Jepsen testing library and the Conductor Java SDK at version 5.0.1. We used this harness to test Orkes Conductor 5.3.2, 5.4.0, and 5.5.0-rc1 and -rc2.

Orkes typically deploys Conductor in cloud environments with Postgres (or a Postgres-compatible database, like their in-house ParticleDB ) as the primary database, and Redis (or a compatible service like Valkey ) as the queue. To approximate these deployments, we set up clusters of ten Debian machines, both in containers and as separate EC2 VMs: a single Postgres node for the database, either a single Redis node or Redis Cluster for the queue, and the remaining nodes split evenly between Conductor servers, Conductor’s standard workers, and a custom worker we wrote using the Java SDK.

Our test workload defined a single workflow with one task, handled by our custom worker. The task slept up to 30 seconds to simulate work being done, then returned a randomly generated output . It also logged its execution with the test harness, so we could tell exactly which tasks had run and when, along with their observed inputs and intended outputs.

Our test proceeded in three phases. During the main phase , the test harness called startWorkflow() with unique inputs (to distinguish executions from one another), kept track of which executions were in-progress and which were terminal, and checked the status of specific executions using getWorkflow() . To discover executions when the call to startWorkflow() timed out or failed, we periodically called getRunningWorkflow() to list all in-progress executions. During the main phase we also injected a variety of faults , including pausing and killing processes, as well as network partitions between Conductor servers and Postgres, Redis, and worker nodes.

During the recovery phase , the test ended network partitions, restarted and unpaused processes, etc., then let the cluster recover. To figure out when the system had converged on a steady state, we polled the depth of Conductor’s decider queue. When this queue reached zero, Conductor had nothing more to do and the test moved to the final phase.

During the final phase , the test read the state of every workflow execution it had ever seen. We then searched for a variety of unexpected behaviors :

Under normal operation, healthy Conductor clusters occasionally executed the same task for the same workflow execution on two workers concurrently. This is not surprising, since mutual exclusion is impossible in asynchronous networks . However, it is worth keeping in mind that even very short-lived tasks may be executed at the same time! In this test run , workflow 3919784b-7691-11f1-a292-00163e983f22 ’s single task began on worker n9 at 70.110 seconds, then on worker n10 at 70.113 seconds. It completed on n9 at 70.114 seconds, and on n10 less than a millisecond later.

The documentation for Conductor OSS describes a distributed locking system which “prevents race conditions when multiple server instances evaluate the same workflow concurrently”. Orkes Conductor also has a locking mechanism whose lease time is configured by conductor.workflow.lockLeaseTime . While this lock can reduce the frequency of concurrent execution, it cannot prevent it entirely.

With our single-task workflows, the default lease time of one minute, two Conductor servers, three workers, near-zero network latency, short-lived tasks (p50 ~500 µs, p95 ~5 ms, p99 ~10 ms), and roughly 1,100 workflows per second, we observed concurrent execution roughly once every six hours in healthy clusters. Reducing the lease time to one second allowed concurrent execution every few minutes. Production frequency may vary.

This problem was exacerbated by a time of check to time of use bug in the sweeper process which re-enqueues stuck tasks. Imagine a sweeper reads a task in state SCHEDULED . A worker then executes that task, changing its state in the database to IN_PROGRESS and removing the task message from the queue. The sweeper then checks the queue and finds no message for the (no longer) scheduled task; it re-enqueues it, leading to duplicate delivery. Orkes reports this issue ( #1 ) is fixed in version 5.5.6.

items.title: L’endorsement di Trump aiuterà Netanyahu alle elezioni israeliane?
items.summary: Meno che in passato, probabilmente, perché Trump non è più popolare come un tempo in Israele, dopo mesi di litigi e disaccordi
items.content:
La scelta di Donald Trump di appoggiare esplicitamente il primo ministro israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu alle elezioni israeliane del 27 ottobre potrebbe essere inefficace, o comunque meno incisiva rispetto agli endorsement che altri presidenti statunitensi avevano fatto in passato a candidati israeliani.

Negli ultimi mesi i rapporti tra Trump e Netanyahu sono stati molto altalenanti, e l’immagine di Trump in Israele è cambiata . Sono emersi i disaccordi sugli obiettivi che i due paesi si erano dati con la guerra all’Iran, e le ultime lodi di Trump a Netanyahu sono state rese meno credibili dai loro litigi pubblici , con tanto di insulti. Trump era arrivato a dire che Netanyahu fosse «impazzito» o a vantarsi di dargli ordini.

L’influenza di Trump nella politica israeliana è legata soprattutto a ciò che porta in dote: l’appoggio militare degli Stati Uniti, un alleato imprescindibile per la sicurezza di Israele. È un aspetto che Trump ha citato nel post melenso in sostegno a Netanyahu: se Israele avesse un leader diverso, ha scritto, gli Stati Uniti sarebbero riluttanti a «finire il lavoro» con l’Iran.

Per esempio l’ex primo ministro centrista Yair Lapid ha detto che «invece di fare pressione su Trump per attaccare l’Iran, Netanyahu l’ha supplicato di fare un post in suo sostegno prima delle elezioni». Anche il generale Gadi Eisenkot, il principale rivale di Netanyahu, ha ringraziato Trump per l’appoggio militare a Israele, sostenendo però che gli Stati Uniti lavoreranno con qualunque governo israeliano eletto democraticamente.

Sui media israeliani ci sono letture altrettanto caute. Principalmente si sono chiesti se l’ endorsement di Trump può davvero aiutare Netanyahu a colmare lo svantaggio: i sondaggi danno ancora la coalizione di estrema destra del primo ministro sotto la maggioranza.

In Israele la fiducia e l’ammirazione per Trump sono ai minimi storici , specie per il modo incoerente in cui il presidente statunitense ha gestito le trattative col regime iraniano e la sequela di ultimatum o annunci trionfalistici sulla riapertura dello stretto di Hormuz. Gli obiettivi israeliani – rendere l’Iran inoffensivo a costo di destabilizzare il Medio Oriente – non si conciliano con le concessioni che Trump si è mostrato disposto a fare al regime.

Un cartellone elettronico di Tel Aviv ringrazia Donald Trump nei primi giorni della guerra iniziata da Stati Uniti e Israele contro l’Iran, il 12 marzo 2026 (AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg)

Il Jerusalem Post ha riconosciuto che comunque Trump è « un grosso calibro » nella campagna elettorale, perché il suo intervento ha condizionato il racconto degli ultimi giorni. Il Times of Israel ha scritto che il principale effetto è stato distogliere, almeno per qualche ora, l’attenzione dalle difficoltà di politica interna di Netanyahu e rimetterla sulla politica estera e sulle guerre, su cui come visto c’è consenso trasversale ma anche un certo scetticismo su Trump.

Haaretz , il giornale più autorevole e il terzo più letto in Israele, ha concluso che è un’operazione rischiosa . Da questo punto di vista, Trump ha dimostrato un certo scollamento dalla campagna elettorale israeliana, che è ancora molto concentrata sull’attentato di Hamas del 7 ottobre 2023 e soprattutto su quanto Netanyahu sapesse e abbia fatto per prevenirlo. Inoltre nelle elezioni è centrale la figura di Netanyahu, che per l’opposizione è corrotto e interessato solo a restare al potere a qualunque costo.

Altre letture si sono domandate, visto l’approccio transazionale di Trump alla diplomazia, che cosa abbia chiesto in cambio a Netanyahu. Secondo Yediot Aharonot , un giornale centrista tra i più letti, l’amministrazione Trump avrebbe chiesto al governo israeliano di rigare dritto, e cioè di non fare attacchi od operazioni militari eclatanti fino alle elezioni di metà mandato del 3 novembre negli Stati Uniti.

In generale, è probabile che l’appoggio di Trump conti soprattutto per l’elettorato di destra radicale, che però avrebbe votato Netanyahu in ogni caso. È ormai anche arcinota la volubilità di Trump, che solo pochi giorni prima del post diceva in un’intervista televisiva di non potersi fidare di Netanyahu. In un’intervista successiva al post è stato ambiguo, dicendo che potrebbe pure collaborare con un diverso leader israeliano, ma «chi vuole correre il rischio?».

Anche il ricatto sugli aiuti militari lascia il tempo che trova: a Trump restano due anni di mandato e altri membri della sua amministrazione, a partire dal vicepresidente JD Vance , si sono rifiutati di appoggiare Netanyahu. Secondo fonti di Haaretz , l’entourage del primo ministro lavorava da tempo per ottenere l’ endorsement di Trump, ma non si aspettava di farcela.

Poche ore prima del post, Netanyahu sosteneva che Israele avrebbe dovuto diversificare le alleanze storiche, guardando a India e America Latina.

Già nel 2013 , prima di entrare in politica, Trump girò un video in sostegno del primo ministro israeliano. Nel 2019, durante il primo mandato presidenziale, Trump riconobbe la sovranità israeliana sulle alture del Golan (al confine con la Siria) poco prima delle elezioni israeliane. Un anno fa ha chiesto pubblicamente al presidente israeliano Isaac Herzog di concedere la grazia a Netanyahu per il processo in cui è imputato per frode e corruzione , e che potrebbe interrompere la sua carriera politica.

items.title: Publish fake stats, get cited in LLMs
items.summary: Article URL: https://peec.ai/blog/publish-stats-get-cited-the-tactic-that-put-my-data-all-over-the-web Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50165801 Points: 282 # Comments: 161
items.content:
What I learned about AI search when I made up 50,000 stats that got cited by ChatGPT...

About 7 months ago, I launched a website with 50,000 statistics. Every one of them was fake.

Google has forgotten the site exists and deindexed the pages, but ChatGPT hasn't. Since the website went live 7 months ago, it has sent more than 10,000 AI sessions its way. And now more than 330 referring domains, including Shopify, Bluehost, and DHL, link to the site. Its made-up numbers have also ended up in an academic paper and in a bank's investment research.

At Peec AI and in the industry, we talk about GEO and SEO every day, and we keep looking for new tactics. I’ve been working on this stats page one for a long time, sharing pieces of it publicly along the way. Of course, it’s experimental, but the results have been hard to ignore.

The impetus to seed a site with statistics came out of long-running research I've been doing on LLMs, relevance engineering, and grounding (credit to the iPullRank team, Dan Petrovic, and Wil Reynolds).

In the course of my work, I noticed a pattern: as more teams write time-sensitive and breaking content with LLMs, those LLMs have to look for (seemingly) reliable data during their research to fill the gaps in their knowledge. Statistics are often exactly what they’re looking for.

Most GEO advice focuses on one moment: getting your brand into the AI answer. This experiment looks at what happens after the answer, when people take that output and use it, putting it into presentations, adding it to a shopping list, and yes, publishing it on their website.

I didn't come up with the idea for this experiment alone. Hat tip to Seer Interactive, who already published an eye-opening study in August 2025 that got a few thoughts bouncing around in my head. Several months later, those thoughts came together and finally made it to the top of my to-do list. In March 2026, I started working on building the site that would let me test my ideas.

Quick context for anyone who wasn’t following along in real time as I ran this experiment:

I bought a brand-new domain, stateglobe.com, and generated 50,000 statistics pages in a single day with GPT-4.1. The site purports to provide stats on SEO, content marketing, social media, e-commerce, and web technology from 200 countries. Except every number was totally invented. I never checked a single one. I pushed them to the site with a basic AI web design template. This cost me around $30. Later, I added 15,000 listicles on top of the statistics. That was about $20 more, so all in all, this is an experiment that came in at the very low price of about $50.

The reaction when I first shared it was wild. When my friend Kevin featured it in Growth Memo , it reached a much bigger audience. I think people responded so enthusiastically to this work because it showed great results while also speaking to the fears people have about what ends up in AI search results.

When I launched the site, traffic, indexing, and engagement were initially going really well. Using indexer tools, I got almost the entire site indexed within a week, and it started to appear in Google results.

Then two Google updates came out right after launch, and my Google visibility collapsed.

I've been invisible on Google for many months now. Indexed pages bounce between 5 and 20 impressions. At one point, I got curious and created a subdomain to see if I could increase impressions, but it didn't really help.

Other than that, I haven't touched the site. Some pages might even fail to load now and then. I don't know.

But when I sat down to write this, I checked the crawl data in Cloudflare after 7 months.

In the last 30 days alone, the site got more than 600,000 requests from bots. Around 72,000 of them came from ChatGPT-User. That is the agent ChatGPT uses to open a page in real time while answering someone. So these are not training crawls. Each one is ChatGPT fetching a fake statistics page to answer a real question.

And when I say, “never stopped,” I mean ChatGPT really never stopped.

According to Ahrefs and Semrush, the site has links from 330+ other sites. That includes well-known brands like Shopify, DHL, and Bluehost. With strong Google performance, the numbers might have been even better.

Google may have forgotten about the site, but ChatGPT clearly hasn’t. The site is still earning citations and traffic more than 7 months after launch.

If you've read Tomek's ChatGPT Index research , you're lucky, because it’s a great intro to how ChatGPT search works. If you haven't, add it to your reading list right now, because it helps explain why my website has been living in ChatGPT/OpenAI Index for so long.

A completely made-up website still performing so well is shocking. Since March, GA4 shows 10,000+ sessions from ChatGPT alone, and Cloudflare shows the site has high marks for retrieval.

I didn’t include direct sessions in overall visits, because it mostly looks like bot traffic. Remember the dead internet theory!

Right after I joined Peec in June 2026, I also set up a visibility dashboard in our tool to track a few prompts. Performance for them is still strong. On October 7, stateglobe.com was ranked second for visibility on these prompts, behind only data powerhouse Statista.

The constant retrieval is the first big lesson: ranking on Google and being retrievable by an LLM are two different problems.

When ChatGPT searches, it doesn't just copy Google's top 10. It rewrites your prompt into its own sub-queries (called fanout queries), pulls candidates from its search sources and its own cache, reranks them, and then opens a handful of pages to ground the answer. A page can be invisible on Google and still perform well in every one of those LLM steps.

StateGlobe is a good example. While Google dropped it, the AI retrieval bots kept coming back.

For GEO, this means Google rankings are only one signal, not the whole picture. If you only track Google, you are missing a channel that can work even when Google says “no.”

You’d expect that if a site performs well with information retrieval tools, its information would begin to appear out in the wild. And you would be right.

StateGlobe was built entirely on fake data, using the cheapest model available and a prompt that was nothing more than a list of countries and topics plus two sentences. Nevertheless, the output was…

…used in investment research by Qatar's largest financial group…

…and used as a source in a research report from a Canadian influencer community.

Note that these are only the citations that linked back to the StateGlobe site. Presumably, many more used the data without a link.

On day one, a fake number on StateGlobe had zero authority. It was a random stat on a brand-new domain.

Then an academic paper cited it. Then a bank. Now the next person, or the next model, that finds this number sees a stat with a source. And that source is cited by serious institutions.

The fake data certainly didn't become true, but every citation made it look more trustworthy.

It has the potential to get worse: after so much retrieval and citation, these pages end up in web crawls, and web crawls end up in training data (I hope it hasn’t!). A number that started as a GPT-4.1 guess can become something the next model "knows."

This points to the larger risk suggested by this experiment, and it's why I'm sharing this as research, not as a playbook for fake content. Verifying sources should become an essential part of writers’ and researchers’ workflows.

Once I began working at Peec, I decided to try a version of this test again. As the GEO Research team, we talked through the results up until that point and quickly launched a simple new page. This time, there were no made-up numbers, and we checked every stat and properly cited its source. You can view it here: peec.ai/ai-search-geo-statistics .

Almost immediately, sites we suspect use AI to write their content started linking to us. For the second time, using a second site, earning links by publishing statistical content proved that a hypothetically strong tactic worked in reality.

The two tests show that LLMs have a strong preference for seeking out statistics when asked to write articles. The mechanism is simple:

When a prompt requires research, the model breaks it into sub-queries, adds modifiers like "statistics," "data," "report," or the current year (if also requested in the prompt text). If someone asks for the model to compose a blog post about remote work, the model will search for "remote work statistics 2026." Pages that optimize for what models search rather than for what humans type will appear more often in LLM results.

When a model is asked to draft a piece of writing, a citation to a page that says "Remote work is growing" adds little authority and remains vague. If that page instead says "X% of employees work remotely at least once a week," there’s suddenly something that is specific, quotable, and additive. When a model grounds an answer, a specific number is the most useful thing it can find. These numbers look like evidence, though as this experiment proves, sometimes they aren’t.

items.title: I messaggi allarmistici circolati tra gli studenti nel Nord Italia
items.summary: Parlavano di violenze e stupri indiscriminati, e in alcune scuole e città sono state prese precauzioni
items.content:
Lunedì sera, tra le chat di studenti delle scuole superiori e delle università di alcune province del Nord Italia, hanno cominciato a circolare messaggi allarmistici che mettevano in guardia su presunte violenze indiscriminate, tra cui stupri di gruppo, che sarebbero state compiute martedì da non si sa bene chi. I messaggi sono circolati molto probabilmente perché ricondotti alle violenze e ai disordini compiuti nel weekend da centinaia di ragazzi giovani a Milano e in misura minore in altre città. Martedì nessuno di questi episodi si è verificato.

Al momento non si sa chi abbia dato inizio a queste catene di messaggi né come si siano diffusi nelle diverse città. Il Post ha chiamato le questure di alcune delle città coinvolte, che hanno detto che la Digos sta conducendo delle indagini soprattutto per capire da chi siano partiti i primi messaggi, ma che in generale li hanno ritenuti infondati.

I messaggi che circolavano tra gli studenti erano spesso confusi e condivisi senza contesto. Non sono circolati screenshot di conversazioni sulla presunta organizzazione di attacchi e stupri (come spesso succede sui social quando esistono per esempio canali Telegram chiusi ma molto frequentati), ma messaggi di persone anonime che raccontavano di avere ricevuto segnalazioni sull’esistenza di questi piani. Molti di questi messaggi sono stati pubblicati anche su TikTok: la maggior parte era riferita a città specifiche, ma i contenuti erano più o meno sempre gli stessi.

Una chat di whatsapp ripresa in un video pubblicato da un utente di TikTok

Contemporaneamente, a partire da lunedì pomeriggio hanno cominciato a circolare su Instagram e in alcuni gruppi WhatsApp anche messaggi su presunte rappresaglie organizzate da gruppi neofascisti per punire gli autori delle violenze di sabato e domenica a Milano. In una di queste si diceva di «picchiare gli stranieri a vista».

I messaggi sono girati soprattutto tra le ragazze per il timore che le minacce di violenze sessuali fossero fondate. Spesso erano accompagnati da frasi come “è importante” o “fate girare”, e in molti casi da un invito a rimanere a casa. Martedì alcuni studenti non sono andati a scuola per paura: è accaduto a Como, Pavia, Verona e Monza.

È probabile che il motivo per cui questi messaggi sono arrivati a circolare così tanto e nel giro di poche ore fosse una già diffusa preoccupazione e attenzione per quanto avvenuto nel weekend.

Nonostante non ci fossero molti elementi per attribuire veridicità a quei messaggi, martedì mattina in alcune città italiane è stato disposto un dispiegamento preventivo di forze dell’ordine per il timore che si verificassero episodi simili a quelli del weekend.

A Chiari, un paese vicino a Brescia, la stazione è stata presidiata fin dal mattino dalle forze dell’ordine, che hanno raccontato che sono arrivati solo pochi gruppi di ragazzi minorenni che sono poi stati rimandati a scuola. A Monza sono state inviate pattuglie di polizia e agenti in borghese vicino alle scuole, ma non è stato segnalato alcun episodio violento.

Una chat di whatsapp ripresa in un video pubblicato da un utente di TikTok

In altri messaggi si parlava di creare scompiglio nelle università di Milano, soprattutto quelle private, per prendersela con le persone ricche che le frequentano. Nelle università comunque le lezioni stanno proseguendo regolarmente senza intoppi. Martedì mattina i rappresentanti dell’organizzazione studentesca Studenti Indipendenti dell’università Bicocca hanno pubblicato una storia su Instagram per rassicurare gli studenti sul fatto che la situazione all’interno dell’università è «tranquilla e normale». Hanno scritto che la veridicità di questi messaggi «è fortemente dubbia» e hanno suggerito di «non alimentare paranoie e odio ingiustificato» condividendo contenuti non ancora verificati.

Messaggi simili sono stati condivisi dai rappresentanti di altre università di Milano, come la Bocconi, mentre gli studenti dell’università IULM e della Cattolica hanno detto di non voler condividere informazioni non verificate e di star aspettando comunicazioni dall’università.

items.title: Dyson porta in Italia i robot Nurovi, con panni triangolari per lavare fino agli angoli
items.summary: L’R1 aspira, l’R2 lava anche i pavimenti. Entrambi si svuotano in una base senza sacco con otto cicloni. Curiosi i “dischi triangolari” ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Dyson ha portato in Italia due nuovi robot aspirapolvere, R1 Nurovi Dry e R2 Nurovi Wash+Dry . Come si intuisce dai nomi, il primo si limita ad aspirare, mentre il secondo lava anche i pavimenti e con panni dalla forma piuttosto insolita .

Al posto dei consueti dischi rotondi, che negli angoli lasciano sempre una porzione di pavimento scoperta, l’R2 usa panni a triangolo di Reuleaux, la figura composta da tre archi di cerchio che mantiene la stessa larghezza in qualunque direzione ruoti . Grazie a un movimento eccentrico le punte del panno arrivano fino alla parete senza perdere la scorrevolezza di un cerchio.

Per l’aspirazione Dyson ha diviso il lavoro con il sistema Twin-capture, in cui le setole della spazzola convogliano dentro i detriti più grossi e lasciano al motore la polvere fine .

La spazzolina laterale si allunga verso i bordi ed è disegnata per non trattenere peli e capelli, mentre un sensore piezoelettrico preso dagli aspirapolvere senza filo della casa rileva la polvere per via acustica e regola la potenza di conseguenza.

A fine ciclo entrambi tornano a una base senza sacco con otto cicloni, che trattiene fino a 90 giorni di sporco secco. Quella dell’R2 lava anche i panni con acqua a 75 °C e li asciuga con aria a 45 °C , mentre programmi e zone di pulizia si gestiscono dall’app MyDyson.

Dyson R1 Nurovi Dry e R2 Nurovi Wash+Dry dono già in vendita rispettivamente a 549 e 849 euro.

items.title: Subaru cambia strada in Europa: addio ai motori boxer dal 2028, poi una piattaforma elettrica proprietaria
items.summary: Outback uscirà di scena già nel 2026, mentre Impreza, Crosstrek e Forester dovrebbero lasciare il mercato europeo nel 2027 ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Per Subaru il passaggio all’auto elettrica in Europa avrà conseguenze particolarmente profonde. Il costruttore giapponese si prepara infatti a eliminare dal Vecchio Continente tutti i modelli con motore a combustione entro il 2028, mettendo fine anche alla lunga storia europea del boxer, uno degli elementi tecnici più strettamente associati al marchio.

Parallelamente, Subaru sta lavorando a una piattaforma elettrica sviluppata internamente, con l’obiettivo di recuperare maggiore autonomia progettuale rispetto alla collaborazione con Toyota. I primi modelli basati sulla nuova architettura potrebbero arrivare dal 2029.

Secondo quanto riportato da Auto Motor und Sport , il processo di uscita dei modelli termici partirà già quest'anno con la Subaru Outback. Nel 2027 dovrebbe essere poi la volta di Impreza, Crosstrek e Forester. Dal 2028, di conseguenza, la gamma Subaru europea sarebbe composta esclusivamente da automobili elettriche.

Per un marchio che ha fatto del motore boxer e della trazione integrale due dei propri tratti distintivi, si tratta di un cambiamento particolarmente significativo. Negli ultimi anni Subaru aveva già accompagnato il boxer con l'elettrificazione leggera del sistema e-Boxer, ma in Europa anche questa soluzione è destinata a scomparire.

La ragione indicata dal costruttore riguarda soprattutto le normative europee sulle emissioni medie di anidride carbonica delle flotte, alle quali si aggiungono requisiti sempre più articolati in materia di sicurezza e sistemi di assistenza alla guida.

Adeguare modelli termici venduti in volumi relativamente contenuti alle nuove normative comporterebbe investimenti che, per un costruttore delle dimensioni di Subaru, rischiano di non essere economicamente sostenibili.

In Europa Subaru punta su Uncharted, Solterra ed e-Outback, modelli che coprono il segmento compatto e quello medio. La strategia però potrebbe richiedere ulteriori ampliamenti della gamma prima del 2028, proprio per compensare l'uscita progressiva dei modelli termici. Su altri mercati è stato già annunciato anche Getaway, SUV elettrico a sette posti che per ora non è previsto in Europa ma che mostra come il catalogo a batteria sia destinato ad ampliarsi ulteriormente.

La transizione europea si appoggia però ancora pesantemente alla collaborazione con Toyota. Solterra è strettamente imparentata con Toyota bZ4X e anche altri modelli elettrici recenti sono stati sviluppati attraverso la partnership tra i due gruppi.

Una collaborazione che ha permesso a Subaru di accelerare l'ingresso nell'elettrico senza sostenere da sola tutti i costi di sviluppo, ma che limita inevitabilmente la libertà di definire ogni elemento tecnico secondo le proprie priorità.

Subaru ha iniziato quindi a testare una nuova architettura proprietaria per i veicoli elettrici nel proprio centro prove a nord di Tokyo. Il prototipo utilizza una carrozzeria modificata di Outback, ma si tratta soltanto di un muletto tecnico e non dell'anticipazione di un modello già destinato alla produzione.

La configurazione sperimentale utilizza due motori elettrici e la trazione integrale, con una potenza complessiva di circa 510 CV. Il motore anteriore sviluppa circa 201 CV, mentre quello posteriore arriva a circa 308 CV. Lo 0-100 km/h richiederebbe meno di quattro secondi.

Le unità sono state sviluppate con Aisin, società legata al gruppo Toyota, ma secondo Subaru sono più piccole e leggere rispetto ai motori utilizzati sulle attuali elettriche. Gli ingegneri indicano un'efficienza superiore di circa il 30% rispetto alla media del settore.

Nel frattempo, da settembre 2024 Subaru sta lavorando con Panasonic Energy a una batteria composta da circa 4.000 celle cilindriche. Il nuovo pacco dovrebbe pesare circa il 25% in meno rispetto alla batteria utilizzata sulle precedenti architetture dell'azienda.

Combinando batteria, motori più compatti e struttura ottimizzata, Subaru punta a ridurre di circa 100 kg il peso complessivo della piattaforma rispetto alle proprie elettriche attuali.

Takatomo Watamori, dirigente dell'area tecnica Subaru, ha spiegato ad Automotive News che avere maggiore controllo sulla tecnologia è considerato fondamentale per preservare caratteristiche come comportamento dinamico, trazione integrale e sicurezza.

items.title: Apple broke an essential presentation feature of iPads
items.summary: Article URL: https://teddysvoronos.com/2026-10-19-apple-broke-an-essential-presentation-feature-of-ipads/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50165208 Points: 395 # Comments: 225
items.content:
A brief digression from my usual teaching posts to complain about a devastating regression in iPadOS 27.

If you’ve followed my work up until now, you’ll know that I rely heavily on writing on handouts from my iPad, projected via AirPlay to an external screen that my students can see. When I’m doing this, my iPad is also doing many other things: controlling a PowerPoint presentation on my Mac , showing me notes that I’ve taken on points I want to mention and students I want to call on, and showing me the results of polls before I reveal them to the class. This ability to do other things on your iPad while the audience just sees your presentation or handout is an essential part of a variety of pedagogical moves that I use in my teaching.

As of iPadOS 27, if you have multiple windows open while AirPlaying (whether or not Stage Manager is on), tapping on anything other than the presenting app will snap the external display into showing your whole iPad screen. This means that my students see all my notes on who I want to call on, or poll results that should be hidden from them. They also get distracted from what we’re learning by all these jarring windows popping up and disappearing. If you’re presenting at a big conference, it’s extremely embarrassing.

In GoodNotes, the presenter view will return once you tap back on the app. In Keynote, it will just exit the presentation entirely. In PowerPoint, it will put the app in a limbo where you have to restart the presentation to proceed. Here’s a Reddit post illustrating the behavior in GoodNotes . But don’t just take my word for it; try it at home!

I sort of understand why Apple did this. In iPadOS 26, which app could “control” the external display was hard to identify. Essentially, you had to swipe up as though going to the home screen, then tap on the app you wanted in the dock, and that app would take over the external display if it had a presentation mode. This was weird and hard to understand, but Apple’s solution is to just make it so that whatever is the most recently tapped app takes over, which is much, much worse.

As for what the behavior should be, I’m not a developer, but here’s a proposal: if you’re using an app that is in presenter mode (e.g., PowerPoint playing a presentation, or a GoodNotes document open), it should always get precedence on the external display, until that presentation gets stopped, the document is closed, or the app is quit. Period.

I talked/griped/whined/begged about this on an episode of Mac Power Users in early September ( here’s a link to the video ), and as of now this behavior hasn’t changed, including in the latest betas. I’m hoping that this post can get the word out, or that maybe someone has figured out a workaround. I’ve also filed a feedback report with Apple and encourage you to do the same ( click here and mention my feedback code FB23615646).

I’ll update this post if anything changes, but for now, I can’t recommend this operating system to anyone using their iPad to teach or present.
